summary_paragraph: A man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, insulin-dependent diabetes, hepatitis C, and a history of cocaine dependence was admitted for acute hypoxic respiratory distress following crack cocaine use. He presented with progressive shortness of breath, cough, and hypoxia requiring BiPAP support. Imaging showed diffuse bilateral lung opacities and new nodular infiltrates, but no evidence of infection on microbiology or clinical course. His respiratory failure was attributed to crack-induced lung injury, consistent with prior episodes. He improved with supportive care including oxygen, nebulizers, and respiratory therapy, without need for intubation, steroids, or antibiotics. His diabetes was managed with increased Lantus insulin to 50 units nightly for better control. Heart failure was stable on home medications. He was discharged home after six days, ambulating independently on room air, with plans for outpatient follow-up for pulmonary, addiction, and hepatitis C care.
problems: Acute pulmonary syndrome (presumably related to crack-cocaine use)
Acute on chronic exacerbation of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy
